title: A line of text, character by character

prereqs.why: The whole problem is reading a line into a std::string and walking its characters.
A range-for over the string is the loop that removes every chance of running off the end.
Each character is classified by a small chain of comparisons.

statement:
Read **one whole line** of input, spaces included, and print:

```
letters <how many ASCII letters>
digits <how many ASCII digits 0-9>
other <everything else, spaces included>
upper [<the line with lowercase letters turned uppercase>]
```

The square brackets are literal, so an empty line is unambiguous.

```
input:   Cache line 64!

output:  letters 9
         digits 2
         other 3
         upper [CACHE LINE 64!]
```

Nine letters, two digits, and three others: two spaces and the `!`.

### The point of the problem

`std::cin >> word` stops at the first space, so it cannot read a line. The tool
for that is `std::getline`:

```cpp
std::string line;
std::getline(std::cin, line);
```

And a `std::string` is walkable like an array:

```cpp
for (char c : line) { /* ... */ }
```

A `char` is a **small integer** holding a character code, which is why `c >= 'a'
&& c <= 'z'` is a legal comparison and why `'7' - '0'` gives the number 7.

### A detail that matters more than it looks

The standard library has `std::isupper`, `std::isdigit` and `std::toupper` in
`<cctype>`, and all of them take an `int` whose value must be a valid
`unsigned char` or `EOF`. On most platforms `char` is **signed**, so a byte
above 127 arrives as a negative number and passing it straight in is undefined
behaviour. The fix is a cast:

```cpp
std::toupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))
```

Either approach is accepted here - explicit comparisons, or `<cctype>` with the
cast. The tests include a byte above 127 so that an uncast version is at least
visibly on thin ice.

### Boundary cases

An empty line: all three counts 0 and `upper []`. A line of only spaces. A line
with no letters. Characters already uppercase, which must stay as they are and
still count as letters. A line containing a non-ASCII byte, which counts as
`other` and is passed through unchanged.

### Platform assumptions

Input is bytes, and "letter" and "digit" mean the ASCII ranges `A-Z`, `a-z` and
`0-9` only. The runner uses the C locale, so no locale-dependent classification
is in play. A byte above 127 is counted as `other` and copied through
untouched - this problem does not decode UTF-8, so a multi-byte character
counts as several `other`s, which is stated here rather than left for you to
discover.
hints: `std::getline(std::cin, line)` reads up to and including the newline, and stores everything before it. Unlike `>>` it keeps the spaces, and it does not skip a leading one.
A range-for is the loop you want: `for (char c : line)`. Build the uppercased result into a second `std::string` with `push_back`, or copy the line first and modify it in place.
To uppercase by hand: if `c >= 'a' && c <= 'z'` then `c = static_cast<char>(c - 'a' + 'A')`. That works because the ASCII lowercase letters are contiguous and so are the uppercase ones.
